# Rethinking artificial-intelligence literacy through the lens of teacher educators: The adaptive AI model

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

### Liat Eyal

_Levinsky-Wingate Academic Center, HaShaked 8, Giv’at Shmuel, Israel_

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into educational settings, models for measuring related 

Artificial-Intelligence Literacy literacy among both teachers and students are rapidly emerging. Yet despite their strengths and benefits, many AI Competencies impose fixed competency levels or overlook contextual factors. Using design-based research, and with the Design-Based Research

participation of 22 higher-education teacher educators, this study critiques existing models and introduces the 

Reflective questionnaire Teacher Education novel Adaptive Artificial-Intelligence-Literacy Model (AALM), grounded in case-study analysis. This evaluation 

framework highlights the dynamic, multi-dimensional nature of artificial-intelligence literacy, organized around three inter-related core axes: contextual fitness, professional needs, and dynamic development. A reflective self- assessment tool is also presented, enabling teachers to evaluate their own artificial-intelligence literacy. This framework offers practical guidance for educational policy and teacher development, advocating for assessment approaches that consider social and cultural contexts, professional needs, and the evolving nature of skills amid rapid technological change. Finally, the case studies illustrate the model’s relevance across diverse educational 

settings.

However, this theo- retical review predates the widespread adoption of generative AI and presents a generic universal framework, while overlooking cultural and social factors that may impact literacy implementation. Moreover, its reliance on Bloom’s taxonomy renders continuous adaptation and revision challenging.

### _Pedagogical integrative models for AI literacy_

Such models view learning as an experiential process that combines technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge, while emphasizing ability, motivation, and ethical responsibility – as per the learners’ developmental stage. They integrate technical, social, and ethical di- mensions of AI learning, fostering research and higher-order thinking skills through active learning. Rather than introducing AI as a stand- alone subject, it is embedded within existing disciplines \[[14\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition). Grounded in the self-determination theory \[[15\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition), these models also promote learner autonomy, belonging, and competence, enhancing both technical expertise and socio-cognitive skills \[[16\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition). Building on Koehler and Mishra’s \[[17\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) framework, Celik \[[18\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) proposes the Intelligent-TPACK frame- work, adding the ethical dimension to the four previously existing ones. Hava & Babayigit ˘ \[[19\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) found positive associations between teachers’ digital proficiency and AI-TPACK competencies, including AI integra- tion in teaching. Using structural equation modeling, they also demon- strate that digital proficiency significantly predicts teachers’ AI-TPACK competencies.

### _Importance of the socio-cultural context_

In an era where AI increasingly permeates education and society, understanding socio-cultural contexts is essential for effective, ethical, and meaningful application in education. In her critical examination of 17 frameworks for assessing AI literacy in elementary schools, Yim \[[5\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) found that these tools tend to focus on constructivist and technical perspectives, while neglecting ethical and social aspects. To bridge this gap, she proposes an intelligence-based framework, viewing AI thinking as a novel cognitive process that emerges from human-AI interactions. This model combines cognitive, creative, and critical thinking, while addressing social, ethical, and environmental concerns. Grounded in Vygotsky’s \[[7\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) socio-cultural theory, it also introduces an inter-disciplinary approach, designed to empower young learners. In their AI-skills model, Miao & Shiohira \[[20\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) outline 18 core skills for teachers across five domains: AI fundamentals, pedagogical strate- gies and integration, ethical considerations, practical application, and ongoing professional development. They also outline four core skills for students: technical knowledge, practical application, ethical awareness, and critical evaluation. However, as noted by the authors, these frameworks were not developed in collaboration with practicing teachers.

Collaborating with teachers, Filo et al. \[[21\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) developed a rubric comprised of four key areas: identifying AI mechanisms, conscious AI use, agency through proactive value-driven application, and ethical consideration. However, this rubric is designed for teachers and students alike, making it more generalized than models like Falloon’s \[[22\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) teacher digital competence framework. In contrast, Ding et al. \[[23\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) employed a context-based approach to AI literacy for pre-service teachers through case-based learning. This method places complex tasks in real-world scenarios, enabling teachers to apply AI knowledge to enhance their learning and professional development.

### _Towards more holistic models_

Heung and Yim \[[24\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) offer guidelines for policymakers and curricu- lum designers to implement holistic AI-literacy education for young learners, equipping them for future challenges. Stolpe & Hallstrom \[¨ [25\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) 

stress context-sensitivity in technological education, offering a frame- work that integrates technical skills, scientific-technological knowledge, and socio-ethical awareness of their impact on individuals and society. Their work expands technological literacy to encompass sub-literacies, such as media and design.

Wang and Lester \[[26\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) and Ng et al. \[[27\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) further explore teacher-specific AI competencies by identifying three core domains: technical, pedagogical, and ethical. Their main contribution is a framework that positions teachers as designers of AI-integrated learning, emphasizing the monitoring and interpreting of student data. Finally, Chan \[[28\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) introduces the dynamic AI-literacy model – a more holistic assessment tool comprised of five AI components – concepts, applica- tions, emotional impact, safety and security, and responsible use – each mapped by literacy levels (low, medium, and high). This model focuses on emotional and ethical aspects, while acknowledging diverse indi- vidual literacy levels amid rapid technological advancements. However, empirical validation is lacking.

The current review highlights shifts in AI-literacy assessment models in education. These changes reflect growing attention to cultural and social contexts, and the need for adaptable tools suited to complex, rapidly evolving technological environments. It also underscores the lack of teacher-focused models that support non-linear skill develop- ment and cultural adaptation. Moreover, existing models often omit technical, pedagogical, ethical, and emotional components, and lack mechanisms for ongoing updates.

### _Research aims and questions_

This study, conducted in collaboration with academic educators with broad digital-learning knowhow, presents a dynamic, context-sensitive framework for assessing AI literacy among teachers. The paper re- views existing models, introduces the proposed framework with case studies – including a reflective assessment model – and offers both theoretical insights and practical tools tailored to diverse educational needs.

The study is guided by the three research questions: 

1. What are the principles, strengths, and limitations of existing AI- literacy assessment models in various educational settings?
2. What are the components of an innovative, context-sensitive model that meets the evolving needs of pre-service and in-service teachers? How do its principles support renewed analysis of diverse educa- tional contexts?
3. What are the key indicators for a teacher’s self-evaluation tool across different educational settings, based on the proposed model?

### Methodology

### _Research-methodology rationale_

Design-based research was selected for this study as it bridges be- tween theory and practice in assessing AI competencies in education. It enables the generating of evidence-based solutions through an iterative cycle of design, implementation, and evaluation (citation omitted; \[[29\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition)). This approach integrates the grounded theory, which offers in- sights into emerging needs \[[30,31\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition), with a systematic design aimed at creating practical outcomes. Its cyclical structure allows continuous refinement, based on feedback from the field, while generating new theoretical understanding \[[32\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition). The ongoing shift between design and implementation supports a model that is rooted in both theory and practice, and enhances research-design efficacy when creating models that merge conceptual depth with real-world applicability.

## Findings

### _Research question 1_

To examine the first research question – What are the principles, strengths, and limitations of existing AI-literacy assessment models in various educational settings? – the participants were asked to identify and analyze relevant frameworks (First Iteration - critical examination and case study analysis). The included articles were recently published (since 2022), empirical, and related to models that were explicitly designed for educational use. These five frameworks represent the most comprehensive and diverse approaches available in the limited litera- ture on AI literacy assessment in education, selected to capture varied theoretical foundations, target audiences, and assessment methodolo- gies. A comparative analysis of the five identified articles is presented in [Table 3,](#model-to-three-diverse-case-studies-where-the-framework-effectively-not-include-quantitative-reliability-testing-or-large-scale-empirical-vali--captured-distinct-ai-literacy-profiles-and-differentiated-between-various-dationethical-considerations) accompanied by illustrative citations from the group discus- sions, and three case studies.

Comparative analysis of the five models presented above reveals several insights (**(based on First Iteration)**. First, they offer varied perspectives of AI literacy, ranging from technical and pedagogical skills \[[21,19\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition) to holistic frameworks that include emotional and ethical di- mensions \[[27\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition). Moreover, despite their comprehensive theoretical foundation, the participants addressed the models’ gaps between theo- retical and practical teacher-training applications. The models also lack specific assessment tools, socio-cultural attention, and practical classroom-implementation guidelines. Synthesis of their strengths and weaknesses underscores the need for a more integrative model that blends theoretical principles with practical tools, and that can be tailored to the evolving needs of teacher education.

To further explore this issue, the current article presents three representative case studies selected from 22 cases shared by partici- pating teacher-educators (emerging from First Iteration dialogues). Based on real dilemmas conveyed by their pre-service and in-service students, these cases illustrate diverse contextual challenges: resource- 

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 2.** The Adaptive AI-Literacy Model (AALM).

limited peripheral settings (Case A), varied pedagogical approaches and subject matters (Case B), and educational leadership contexts (Case C). They serve as the foundation for evaluating existing models and exemplify the broad spectrum of situations encountered in contempo- rary teacher education.

#### _Case-study A_

Mai, a third-year pre-service high-school teacher, works with the Bedouin population in a resource-limited region in the periphery of Israel, where even basic infrastructure is lacking. Classrooms often have no computers or internet access, electricity is unreliable, and not all students have mobile telephones – factors that greatly diminishes her motivation to explore AI tools. Instead, she focuses on developing instructional materials for her students, which are ultimately printed and distributed by hand. She was deliberating whether to learn to create AI bots – a skill that would likely be redundant for her students – or focus on different competencies.

In such settings, traditional AI-literacy assessment tools in education reveal fundamental flaws. They assume a direct link between technology usage and AI literacy, overlooking how minimal yet mindful use may reflect advanced pedagogical insights. Due to their technological bias, these tools place undue emphasis on the use of advanced technologies, while neglecting important pedagogical approaches and cultural con- texts. Furthermore, they often prioritize technical proficiency, while disregarding socio-cultural relevance and educational context. By ignoring social disparities and digital gaps, they risk misjudging teacher capabilities. Their rigid focus on specific skills fails to recognize creative adaptation within constraints. Moreover, their underlying assumption of uniform progress neglects the principle that at times, less is more. True AI literacy lies in meaningful, context-aware application, grounded in a deep understanding of student and community needs.

Based on the adaptive AI-Literacy approach, strategic recommen- dations for Mai’s dilemma include prioritizing competencies suited to current conditions – such as using AI to create culturally relevant ma- terials, developing print-deliverable content, and planning for gradual technology integration. As such, skills that are not immediately appli- cable, such as bot building, should be deferred until infrastructure im- proves. This approach ensures that AI integration is responsive to both context and resources.

#### _Case-study B_

Ruth is an experienced high-school math teacher who specializes in exam preparation. Danny is a novice social-science teacher at an alter- native high school, who teaches through discussion and inquiry, fostering critical thinking about social issues. Ruth needs AI literacy that supports precision, structured problem-solving, and abstract concepts visualization, while Danny needs skills for conducting text analysis, identifying social bias, and navigating ethical concerns. Ruth could benefit from mastering tools like WolframAlpha and Microsoft Math Solver, while Danny should focus on platforms such as NotebookLM and article summarizers.

Current AI-literacy assessment models overlook such differences in teachers’ needs. While they measure usage, understanding, and ethics, the skills that they measure are generic rather than being tailored to specific subject areas or pedagogical approaches. Since AI textual fields evolve faster than mathematical ones, teachers may not need to achieve the same AI-literacy levels. Yet existing models impose uniform re- quirements that may be irrelevant to certain roles. A dynamic contextual assessment, on the other hand, would recognize that Ruth must identify mathematical errors in AI outputs while using AI tools for visual dem- onstrations, while Danny needs to analyze social trends, synthesize diverse sources, and address socio-ethical concerns regarding AI.

#### _Case-study C_

Roni, a high-school principal in a medium-sized city, oversees about 800 students and 70 teachers. She leads efforts to implement

pedagogical innovation while navigating challenges related to inte- grating AI into teaching, learning, and assessments. This case study highlights the limitations of standardized AI-literacy rubrics, that emphasize principles of AI operations, data interpretations, and others – which overlook leadership and management competencies that are critical to her role.

Roni requires strategic and regulatory literacy to help her shape AI school policies, make informed technology-related investments, and understand their systemic impact on teaching, learning, and assessment processes. Contextual approaches, however, could assess her AI literacy in light of her managerial role, emphasizing skills that are required for effectively creating change, building visions, and managing the school in a rapidly evolving educational landscape.

These case studies, derived from real dilemmas shared by partici- pants, informed the development of the model presented below and demonstrated its relevance across diverse educational contexts.

### innovative, context-sensitive model that meets the evolving needs of pre-service and in-service teachers? How do its principles support renewed analysis of diverse educational contexts?

In light of the inadequacy of existing frameworks for assessing AI literacy in education, a new model was developed ([Fig. 2)](#findings) – in collab- oration with the 22 teacher educators who participated in this study ([Table 1)](#innovation-and-digital-learning-design-in-academia-180-h-aimed-at-creation-of-assessment-indicators-and-their-rationales-were-analyzed-to-training-teacher-educators-to-integrate-pedagogical-innovation-and-establish-the-self-evaluation-tools-components-and-structure-advanced-technologies-into-teacher-training-institutions-twenty-two-triangulation-across-data-sources-and-peer-debriefing-through-teacher-education-experts-82--females-were-selected-through-a-participant-validation-ensured-analytical-rigor-36-the-analysis-pro--rigorous-process-based-on-three-criteria-substantial-experience-in-cess-concluded-when-broad-consensus-was-reached-regarding-the-pro--teacher-education-and-technology-integration-a-graduate-degree-64--posed-model-and-its-key-components-aligning-with-the-iterative-held-a-phd-and-strong-digital-and-pedagogical-skills-the-participants-consensus-building-nature-of-the-research-design-represented-diverse-regions-and-sectors-across-israel-from-arab-jewish--state-and-jewish-religious-academic-institutions-table-1-presents-their) (Second and Third Iterations - synthesis and consensus- building) Unlike traditional rubrics with fixed, predefined categories, the proposed model introduces a dynamic, non-linear approach, allowing flexible progression based on individual needs. Its key strength 

lies in capturing the complexity of different educational roles and illustrating how AI literacy evolves across contexts and over time. The model is structured around three inter-related axes. The _context- fit (CF) axis_ includes adaptation to available infrastructure, socio- cultural factors, local needs, and the educator’s developmental stage in AI-literacy. The _professional-needs (PN) axis_ relates to the specific discipline, pedagogical aspects, leadership, and support. Finally, the _dynamic-development (DD) axis_ reflects growth in response to techno- logical advancements, evolving roles, changing needs, and expanding capabilities. Together, these axes provide a flexible framework that aligns AI-literacy assessments with the realities of diverse educational settings.

#### _Overlapping areas_

The three axes are inter-connected, with several areas of overlap reflecting the complex nature of AI literacy. The _context-professional overlap_ (CF\_PN) marks the intersection between local conditions and professional demands. The _professional-dynamic overlap_ (PN\_DD) cap- tures how professional needs evolve over time. Finally, the _dynamic- context overlap_ (DD\_CF) highlights shifts in the educational environment that influence literacy development. At the core of the model lies the _central AI-literacy area_, where context, professional needs, and dynamic development converge, representing the integrated essence of adaptive, meaningful AI literacy.

Unlike existing AI literacy models that adopt linear progression through predetermined stages (e.g., \[43,[4\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition)), the AALM introduces several key innovations that extend beyond traditional one-dimensional perceptions. First, it employs a dynamic, non-linear approach that rec- ognizes different literacy paths for different contexts - acknowledging that a math teacher in a well-equipped urban school requires different AI competencies than a teacher in a resource-limited peripheral setting (as illustrated in Case Study A). Second, while existing models treat tech- nical, pedagogical, and ethical dimensions as separate components, AALM integrates contextual adaptation, professional differentiation, and temporal development as interconnected axes, emphasizing dy- namic interactions between dimensions. Third, the model explicitly addresses infrastructure limitations and socio-cultural factors that pre- vious frameworks largely overlook - a critical gap identified in our analysis of existing models ([Table 3)](#model-to-three-diverse-case-studies-where-the-framework-effectively-not-include-quantitative-reliability-testing-or-large-scale-empirical-vali--captured-distinct-ai-literacy-profiles-and-differentiated-between-various-dationethical-considerations). Finally, unlike predominantly theoretical frameworks, AALM was co-created with diverse teacher ed- ucators through iterative design-based research, ensuring practical applicability across varied educational contexts. A detailed comparison between the models presented in [Table 3](#model-to-three-diverse-case-studies-where-the-framework-effectively-not-include-quantitative-reliability-testing-or-large-scale-empirical-vali--captured-distinct-ai-literacy-profiles-and-differentiated-between-various-dationethical-considerations) and the AALM framework is provided in [Table 4.](#research-question-2)

### _Research question 3_

## Finally, the third research question asked, What are the key in- dicators for a teacher’s self-evaluation tool across different educational settings, based on the proposed model? To address this topic, the re- searchers and participants jointly created a self-assessment tool for teachers and educators ([Table 4)](#research-question-2). Following systematic review of the case studies and the developed model, participants proposed question- naire items aligned with each model component. All items emerged through collaborative dialogue, with participants suggesting specific indicators based on their analysis of real-world scenarios. The ques- tionnaire underwent iterative refinement through shared document editing and consensus-building discussions until final agreement was reached (Fourth Iteration - collaborative questionnaire development) ([Table 5)](#research-question-2).

## Discussion

The aim of this study was to critically review models for assessing AI literacy in education and propose a more adaptable framework that also accounts for socio-cultural contexts. Some models build on established 

frameworks for defining learning-complexity levels (Touretzky et al.), while incorporating various literacy elements – from basic knowledge to ethics and critical thinking \[[21\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition). Others, like the AI-TPACK, integrate technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge \[[19\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition).

However, they pose key challenges, including ambiguous definitions of AI literacy that hinder assessment validity \[[21\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition). These initial evalu- ation approaches, which were at the core of the "first wave," (e.g., \[[4\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition)), tend to overemphasize technical knowledge at the expense of social and ethical considerations, while offering limited adaptability options for addressing diverse educational settings \[[42\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition). Additional difficulties stem from the rapid AI evolution, a shift in teachers’ competencies, and the need to balance a range of skills while addressing the educator’s role, experience, and expectations. This underscores the importance of developing a more dynamic and context-sensitive approach. The proposed AALM introduces an innovative paradigm for conceptualizing and assessing AI literacy in education, structured around three interrelated axes: (1) context fit (adaptation to available infrastructure, socio-cultural environments, local priorities, and devel- opmental stage); (2) professional needs (subject-specific instructional demands, pedagogical needs, leadership and managerial re- sponsibilities, and support mechanisms); and (3) dynamic development (evolution in response to technological advancements, shifting roles, emerging needs, and developing competencies).

### _The context-fit / professional-needs axes overlap_

The intersection of the context-fit and professional-needs axes re- flects a dynamic interaction between environmental-cultural-social factors and demands of the educational profession. It is within this space that educators tailor their AI knowledge to their specific opera- tional context. The above field analysis reveals various expressions of this in practice: Teachers in peripheral regions devise strategies for adapting AI tools to infrastructure limitations, illustrating how the drive for innovation is shaped by contextual constraints. Similarly, educa- tional leaders who serve distinct populations must craft AI usage policies that align with community values, while promoting pedagogical advancement.

The context-fit / professional-needs overlap highlights how AI lit- eracy does not develop in isolation, but is shaped by the educator’s specific context. This perspective aligns with socio-cultural perspectives of learning and professional growth \[[7,35\]](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition), whereby knowledge and skills are perceived as outcomes of continuous socio-cultural in- teractions. This overlap also challenges conventional models that emphasize standardization and uniform skill sets, offering a differenti- ated approach that values the uniqueness of each educational setting. The intersection of context and needs is not just a space for adaptation, but also a platform for pedagogical creativity and innovative use of AI in education. Finally, this overlap underscores the need for a nuanced multi-dimensional approach to assessing AI literacy – one that accounts for the complex environment in which educators work, beyond their technical or pedagogical knowledge \[[39,](#future-directions-10-thelen-e-smith-lb-a-dynamic-systems-approach-to-the-development-of-cognition)44\]. This perspective marks an important step towards more targeted professional–development programs.

### _The professional-needs / dynamic-development axes overlap_

The overlap between these two axes illustrates how the AI needs of educators develop over time. This reflects the understanding that AI literacy is a continuous process that is shaped by technological inno- vation, changing roles, and professional growth. Such progression is evident in the case-study analysis presented above, where the math teacher initially used basic AI tools for checking exercises, yet later adopted more advanced technologies for visual demonstrations that enrich teaching and learning. This shift reflects both increased technical proficiency and a broader perspective on how technology can support subject instruction. Theoretical significance of this overlap lies in 

viewing AI literacy as a process of continuous learning and adjustments 

Finally, this overlap emphasizes the need for "literacy agility" – i.e., the capacity for continuous adaptation to context. Practically, this calls for cultivating educators’ meta-cognitive abilities and reflective thinking, to support adaptive responses in shifting operational contexts.

### _The core AI-literacy zone_

At the center of the AALM – where contextual adaptation, profes- sional needs, and dynamic development intersect – lies the core AI lit- eracy dimension. This zone represents optimal AI literacy in educational settings, characterized by full integration and balanced interactions between the model’s three central dimensions. Understanding this area offers valuable insights into effective and transformative AI use in educational settings.

One key feature is the seamless integration of context, needs, and development. In this zone, educators align their understanding of their socio-cultural environment with the clear identification of professional needs and awareness of growth processes. Another defining aspect is that AI use becomes authentic and deeply embedded in teaching, with literacy reaching its highest impact and relevance. The case-study analysis reveals that educators in this zone design rich, meaningful pedagogical practices that enhance learning. Strong adaptability is another core trait. Here, educators respond swiftly and efficiently to technological, contextual, and professional change. This flexibility stems from expertise, systemic awareness, and meta-cognitive skills, enabling 

fluid navigation across the three axes – an essential capability in a fast- 

### _Contribution to the educational field_

This study offers meaningful multi-dimensional contributions to education across three key domains. First, the AALM model presents an innovative theoretical framework for understanding AI literacy as context-dependent, capturing the complexity of educational settings and their related resources, opportunities, and constraints – a reality that policymakers must consider. Second, the model’s integrative perspec- tive has important implications for professional development and teacher training in relation to AI. Rather than narrowly focusing on technical skills, training should foster the ability to integrate multiple dimensions and promote systemic, reflective awareness. The findings suggest that effective professional development requires authentic practice, ongoing reflection, and supportive learning communities – enabling educators to gradually achieve comprehensive and effective AI literacy.

Finally, the proposed self-assessment tool could enable educators to evaluate their own AI literacy, through a dynamic, context-specific lens. It addresses adaptation to local conditions (e.g., infrastructure and cul- tural alignment), professional needs (such as subject-specific pedagogy), and evolving skill development. Complementing the self-assessment questionnaire – with items such as "I adapt AI use to my students’ cul- tural characteristics" or "I select AI tools that are appropriate for my taught subject " – encourages critical reflection and directly supports the development of the literacy that it measures.
